payload.holding: The Tribunal held the insurance company liable to pay compensation to the three injured claimants after deducting 50% for contributory negligence due to driving without a license and helmets.
payload.ratio: In motor accident claim cases under Section 166 of the MV Act, the standard of proof is based on preponderance of probabilities, and police record documents such as the FIR and charge sheet are sufficient to establish negligence in the absence of rebuttal. Furthermore, contributory negligence is established when the injured rider is proven to have been driving without a valid driving license and without wearing a helmet.

in the scheme of the Act and when read together mean: (1) it is legally obligatory to ensure the
Motor Vehicle against third party risk. Driving an uninsured vehicle is an offence punishable with an
imprisonment extending up to three months or the fine which may extend to Rs. 1,000 or both; (2)
policy of insurance must comply with the requirement as contained in Section 147 of the Act; (3) it is
obligatory for the insurer to satisfy the judgment and awards against the person insured in respect
of third party risks. These are Sub-sections (1) and (7) of Section 149. Grounds on which insurer can

that he has done the fair thing". The amount awarded must not be niggardly since the "law values
life and limb in a free society in generous scales". All this means that the sum awarded must be fair

payload.holding: The appeal of the insurance company is dismissed, and the appeal of the claimants is partly allowed by setting aside the finding of contributory negligence, factoring in future prospects, and enhancing the total compensation to Rs. 13,74,876/- with a pay-and-recover order against the vehicle owner.

args.question: Compensation for death of a 16-year-old pillion rider (minor, no income) killed when a bus hit the motorcycle, and the bus operator's defence that the boy contributed by not wearing a helmet.

supporting.title: Sangeeta Devi vs Mahesh Chand & Ors
supporting.principle: For death of a child with no proven earnings, compensation is computed using inflation-corrected notional income of Rs. 15,000 p.a. (Second Schedule), deducting 1/3rd for personal expenses, applying an age-appropriate multiplier, and adding an equal amount as composite non-pecuniary damages (RK Malik formula).
supporting.fact_alignment: Deceased was a 10-year-old child with no income; our client's son is a 16-year-old minor with no income. Both involve death claims under Section 166 MV Act where the child had no proven earnings.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the direct authority for how to compute compensation for a deceased minor. For a 16-year-old (age group >15 but <18), the multiplier is 18 (not 10 as for a 10-year-old). The formula yields a significantly higher award than the standard Sarla Verma framework for zero-income adults.
supporting.quote: For Children of the age group of more than 15 years but less than 18 years, the loss to estate shall be calculated by applying the multiplier of eighteen (18). After the pecuniary loss to estate has been worked out... an amount equivalent to the amount thus computed shall be added to it as the composite non pecuniary damages taking care of not only the conventional heads but also towards future prospects as awarded in R. K. Malik V/s Kiran Pal (2009) 14 SCC 1.

supporting.title: The Oriental Insurance Comp. Ltd. vs Smt. Rani And Ors.
supporting.principle: The burden of proving contributory negligence lies on the party asserting it (the insurer). Mere assertion without evidence is insufficient; the insurer must lead evidence to discharge this burden.
supporting.fact_alignment: In our case, the bus operator/insurer will assert contributory negligence for not wearing a helmet. This case holds that the burden is on them to prove it. The deceased was a pillion rider, not the driver — the insurer must show how the pillion rider's lack of a helmet caused or contributed to the accident.
supporting.why_it_matters: This shifts the evidentiary burden to the insurer. They cannot simply allege contributory negligence; they must lead evidence. Since the deceased was a pillion rider (not controlling the motorcycle), proving that his lack of a helmet contributed to the bus hitting the motorcycle is very difficult.
supporting.quote: Since the plea of contributory negligence was taken by the appellant... therefore, burden of proving the fact of contributory negligence was on the part of the driver of the Motorcycle... even initial burden to prove own pleadings is not discharged by the appellant as no documentary evidence has been produced.

supporting.title: National Insurance Company Ltd. vs Smt. Meena And 4 Others
supporting.principle: A finding of contributory negligence cannot be based on assumptions from a police sketch/site plan when there is consistent oral testimony of an eye-witness establishing absence of negligence on the deceased's part.
supporting.fact_alignment: The insurer may try to argue contributory negligence based on the accident site plan or police documents. This case holds that such documents cannot override consistent eye-witness testimony that the deceased was not negligent.
supporting.why_it_matters: If our client can produce an eye-witness (e.g., the motorcycle rider who survived, or a bystander) who testifies that the bus driver was solely at fault, the tribunal cannot infer contributory negligence from a site plan or from the mere fact that the pillion rider had no helmet.
supporting.quote: Where there is consistent and unimpeached oral testimony of an eye-witness establishing the absence of negligence on the part of the deceased, a tribunal cannot record a finding of contributory negligence merely by drawing assumptions from a police sketch or site plan.

supporting.title: Suman Lata And Ors. vs Madan Mohan Sonkar And Ors.
supporting.principle: When a vehicle hits another from behind, the maxim res ipsa loquitur applies, and the question of contributory negligence does not arise.
supporting.fact_alignment: If the bus hit the motorcycle from behind (as is common in such accidents), res ipsa loquitur applies. The bus driver's negligence is self-evident, and no contributory negligence can be attributed to the pillion rider.
supporting.why_it_matters: This provides a powerful argument if the facts support it. A rear-end collision by a bus against a motorcycle makes the bus driver's negligence self-evident, and the pillion rider's helmet status becomes irrelevant to causation.
supporting.quote: The finding, which is based on correct and proper appraisal of the evidence makes the maxim of res ipsa loquitur applicable to the facts of the present case because the things are so apparent that the question of contributory negligence does not arise.

adverse.title: Kamal S/O Shiv Ram vs Mursleem S/O Mohd. Akil
adverse.principle: Contributory negligence is established when the injured rider is proven to have been driving without a valid driving license and without wearing a helmet, warranting a 50% deduction from compensation.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will cite this to argue that the pillion rider's failure to wear a helmet constitutes contributory negligence, and will seek a 50% deduction from the compensation. The case applied a 50% deduction where all three occupants (driver and two pillion riders) were not wearing helmets.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: Critically, in Kamal the 50% deduction was applied primarily because the DRIVER had no licence AND no helmet — the driver's own negligence in riding without a licence was the main cause. The pillion riders' lack of helmets was a secondary factor. In our case, the deceased was a pillion rider (not the driver) and had no control over the motorcycle. A pillion rider's failure to wear a helmet does not cause or contribute to the accident itself — it may only affect the nature/severity of injuries. The insurer must prove that the lack of a helmet caused or contributed to the accident, not just to the injuries. Moreover, the 50% figure is not a fixed rule; it depends on the facts. A much lower deduction (if any) would be appropriate for a pillion rider.
adverse.quote: The contributory negligence of injured is proved in view of testimony of PW-1 Kamal who categorically deposed... that he is the one who was driving the motorcycle... he did not have DL at the time of accident and they all three were not wearing the helmets. Keeping in view of circumstances of the case, the 50% of the total compensation amount is deducted towards contributory negligence.

adverse.title: Liyakat Ali vs Smt Chunni Devi
adverse.principle: Where a vehicle is used for a purpose not covered by the insurance policy (e.g., tractor used for commercial transport), the insurer is not liable.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may argue that if the motorcycle was being used in violation of policy conditions (e.g., carrying a pillion when not permitted, or the rider lacked a licence), they may seek to avoid or limit liability.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case concerns a tractor used for non-agricultural purposes — a policy breach defence. In our case, the claim is against the BUS operator's insurer, not the motorcycle's insurer. The bus is the offending vehicle. The motorcycle's insurance status is irrelevant to the bus insurer's liability to the pillion rider as a third party. The bus insurer's liability to third parties is statutory under Section 149 MV Act.

adverse.title: Shivlal And Ors. vs Smt. Rukmabai And Ors.
adverse.principle: A gratuitous passenger in a goods vehicle is not covered by the insurance policy, and the insurer is not liable for such passengers.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may try to analogise that a pillion rider on a motorcycle is akin to a gratuitous passenger and therefore not covered.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case concerns goods vehicles (where passengers are not permitted). A pillion rider on a motorcycle is a lawful passenger — motorcycles are designed to carry a pillion. Moreover, the claim here is against the BUS insurer, not the motorcycle insurer. The bus is the offending vehicle, and the pillion rider is a third party vis-à-vis the bus. The bus insurer's liability to third parties is absolute under Section 149.

adverse.title: National Insurance Co.Ltd. vs Harpreet Singh And Ors.
adverse.principle: Legal representatives of a deceased who was not earning and had no dependents may still claim compensation, but the quantum is limited to loss to estate, not loss of dependency.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will argue that since the deceased was a 16-year-old minor with no income and no dependents, the compensation should be minimal — limited to loss to estate with no dependency component.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This is actually already accounted for in the RK Malik / Sangeeta Devi framework for child deaths. The Sangeeta Devi formula specifically addresses this by using inflation-corrected notional income (Rs. 15,000 p.a. from the Second Schedule) and applying a multiplier of 18 for the 15-18 age group, plus an equal amount as composite non-pecuniary damages. This yields a substantial award (likely Rs. 8-10 lakhs depending on the year of accident and CII), not a minimal one. The framework is designed precisely for children with no proven earnings.

priority_arguments: Lead with Sangeeta Devi (doc_022) for the compensation framework: the deceased was 16 (>15 but <18), so multiplier is 18, notional income is Rs. 15,000 p.a. inflation-corrected via CII, 1/3rd deduction, plus equal composite non-pecuniary damages. This yields a significantly higher award than the standard adult framework.

On contributory negligence: the burden of proof is on the insurer (doc_018). The deceased was a pillion rider, not the driver — he had no control over the motorcycle. The insurer must prove that the absence of a helmet caused or contributed to the accident, not just to the severity of injuries. This is a very high bar.
If the bus hit the motorcycle from behind, argue res ipsa loquitur (doc_023) — the bus driver's negligence is self-evident and contributory negligence does not arise.
If there is an eye-witness, rely on doc_006 (Meena) to argue that consistent oral testimony cannot be overridden by assumptions from a police sketch or site plan.

The Kamal case (doc_009) is distinguishable: the 50% deduction there was primarily for the driver riding without a licence, and the pillion riders' lack of helmets was a secondary factor. A pillion rider's helmet status does not cause the accident.
strategy.compensation_range: Approximately Rs. 8-12 lakhs (depending on the year of accident and applicable CII), computed as: inflation-corrected notional income (Rs. 15,000 × CII_year/331), rounded, minus 1/3rd personal expenses, × multiplier 18, plus an equal amount as composite non-pecuniary damages. Plus funeral expenses and interest at 9% p.a. from the date of petition.
strategy.compensation_reasoning: Under the RK Malik framework as applied in Sangeeta Devi (doc_022), for a child aged >15 but <18, the multiplier is 18. The notional income of Rs. 15,000 p.a. (Second Schedule) is inflation-corrected using the CII for the financial year of the accident. After deducting 1/3rd for personal expenses, the balance is capitalised using multiplier 18. An equal amount is added as composite non-pecuniary damages (covering conventional heads and future prospects). If the accident occurred in, say, 2024-25 (CII ~ 363), the inflation-corrected notional income would be ~Rs. 16,450 p.a., loss to estate = (16,450 × 2/3 × 18) = ~Rs. 1,97,400, doubled = ~Rs. 3,94,800, plus funeral expenses. However, if the accident is more recent, the CII adjustment yields higher figures.
risks: The insurer will cite Kamal (doc_009) to argue for a 50% contributory negligence deduction for not wearing a helmet. Counter: the deceased was a pillion rider, not the driver; the helmet's absence did not cause the accident.
The insurer will argue that a minor with no income should get minimal compensation. Counter: Sangeeta Devi (doc_022) provides a specific framework for children that yields substantial compensation.

If the motorcycle rider (who survived) is found to have been negligent (e.g., riding without a licence, speeding), the insurer may argue that the pillion rider should have known better. Counter: a 16-year-old pillion rider cannot be expected to assess the driver's competence; the duty to ensure a valid licence is on the rider/driver, not the pillion.
The insurer may challenge the multiplier or the notional income figure. Counter: the multiplier of 18 for age 15-18 is well-established in RK Malik and Sangeeta Devi.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: File a claim petition under Section 166 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 before the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal having jurisdiction over the place of accident. Claim compensation as per the RK Malik / Sangeeta Devi framework. Also claim interim compensation under Section 140 (no-fault liability) of Rs. 50,000, which is payable regardless of negligence.

caveats: The corpus does not contain any Supreme Court judgment directly holding that a pillion rider's failure to wear a helmet constitutes contributory negligence. The only case on point (Kamal, doc_009) is a Tribunal-level decision where the 50% deduction was driven primarily by the driver's lack of a licence, not solely by the helmet issue.

The corpus does not contain any judgment quantifying the exact compensation for a 16-year-old deceased minor using the RK Malik framework. Sangeeta Devi (doc_022) applied it to a 10-year-old; the principles are directly transferable but the specific figures will depend on the CII for the year of the accident.

No judgment in the corpus addresses the specific question of whether a pillion rider's failure to wear a helmet can be contributory negligence when the accident was caused solely by the bus driver's negligence (e.g., the bus hit the motorcycle). The causation chain is critical: lack of a helmet does not cause the accident, it may only affect injury severity.

The corpus does not contain any judgment from the Supreme Court or a High Court on the helmet-contributory-negligence point specifically for pillion riders. The available authority is from a Motor Accident Claims Tribunal (doc_009), which has persuasive but not binding value.

payload.title: United India Insurance Co Ltd., vs Smt Parvathi Hebbar W/O Late ...
payload.court: In The High Court Of Karnataka At Bengaluru
payload.holding: The Court held that where a driving license is renewed more than 30 days after its expiry, it takes effect from the date of renewal and does not cover the interregnum period of the accident, but directed the insurance company to satisfy the award and recover the amount from the insured owner under the 'pay and recover' principle.
payload.ratio: When an application for renewal of a driving license is made more than 30 days after its expiry, the license is renewed from the date of renewal; thus, the driver does not hold a valid license on the date of an accident occurring during the lapsed period, absolving the insurer of primary liability, though a 'pay and recover' order may be issued in favour of third-party claimants.

payload.court: High Court of Himachal Pradesh, Shimla

payload.ratio: Merely because a passenger falls from a bus while boarding, no presumption of criminal negligence can be drawn against the driver in the absence of evidence showing he moved the vehicle suddenly without signal or proper care. Furthermore, the absence of a driving licence does not in itself constitute rashness or negligence in driving.

payload.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
payload.court: In The High Court Of Judicature At Madras
payload.holding: The Court held that while the driver did not possess a specific endorsement to drive a heavy goods vehicle (having only a light motor vehicle licence with a transport vehicle endorsement), in third-party insurance claims, the insurer must indemnify the victim and is entitled to a pay-and-recover order against the vehicle owner.
payload.ratio: In third-party motor accident claims, even if the driver lacks an appropriate endorsement to drive a specific heavy vehicle class (possessing only an LMV/transport endorsement), the insurer remains liable to satisfy the third-party award and may recover the amount from the insured owner.

args.question: Compensation for death of a 16-year-old pillion rider (minor, no income) killed when a bus hit the motorcycle, and the bus operator's defence that the boy contributed by not wearing a helmet.

supporting.title: Sangeeta Devi vs Mahesh Chand & Ors
supporting.principle: For death of a child with no proven earnings, compensation is computed using inflation-corrected notional income of Rs. 15,000 p.a. (Second Schedule), deducting 1/3rd for personal expenses, applying an age-appropriate multiplier, and adding an equal amount as composite non-pecuniary damages (RK Malik formula).
supporting.fact_alignment: Deceased was a 10-year-old child with no income; our client's son is a 16-year-old minor with no income. Both involve death claims under Section 166 MV Act where the child had no proven earnings.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the direct authority for computing compensation for a deceased minor. For a 16-year-old (age group >15 but <18), the multiplier is 18. The formula yields a substantially higher award than the standard Sarla Verma framework for zero-income adults.
supporting.quote: For Children of the age group of more than 15 years but less than 18 years, the loss to estate shall be calculated by applying the multiplier of eighteen (18). After the pecuniary loss to estate has been worked out... an amount equivalent to the amount thus computed shall be added to it as the composite non pecuniary damages taking care of not only the conventional heads but also towards future prospects as awarded in R. K. Malik V/s Kiran Pal (2009) 14 SCC 1.

supporting.title: The Oriental Insurance Comp. Ltd. vs Smt. Rani And Ors.
supporting.principle: The burden of proving contributory negligence lies on the party asserting it (the insurer). Mere assertion without evidence is insufficient; the insurer must lead evidence to discharge this burden.
supporting.fact_alignment: In our case, the bus operator/insurer will assert contributory negligence for not wearing a helmet. This case holds that the burden is on them to prove it. The deceased was a pillion rider, not the driver — the insurer must show how the pillion rider's lack of a helmet caused or contributed to the accident.
supporting.why_it_matters: This shifts the evidentiary burden to the insurer. They cannot simply allege contributory negligence; they must lead evidence. Since the deceased was a pillion rider (not controlling the motorcycle), proving that his lack of a helmet contributed to the bus hitting the motorcycle is very difficult.
supporting.quote: Since the plea of contributory negligence was taken by the appellant... therefore, burden of proving the fact of contributory negligence was on the part of the driver of the Motorcycle... even initial burden to prove own pleadings is not discharged by the appellant as no documentary evidence has been produced.

supporting.title: National Insurance Company Ltd. vs Smt. Meena And 4 Others
supporting.principle: A finding of contributory negligence cannot be based on assumptions from a police sketch/site plan when there is consistent oral testimony of an eye-witness establishing absence of negligence on the deceased's part.
supporting.fact_alignment: The insurer may try to argue contributory negligence based on the accident site plan or police documents. This case holds that such documents cannot override consistent eye-witness testimony that the deceased was not negligent.
supporting.why_it_matters: If our client can produce an eye-witness (e.g., the motorcycle rider who survived, or a bystander) who testifies that the bus driver was solely at fault, the tribunal cannot infer contributory negligence from a site plan or from the mere fact that the pillion rider had no helmet.
supporting.quote: Where there is consistent and unimpeached oral testimony of an eye-witness establishing the absence of negligence on the part of the deceased, a tribunal cannot record a finding of contributory negligence merely by drawing assumptions from a police sketch or site plan.

supporting.title: Suman Lata And Ors. vs Madan Mohan Sonkar And Ors.
supporting.principle: When a vehicle hits another from behind, the maxim res ipsa loquitur applies, and the question of contributory negligence does not arise.
supporting.fact_alignment: If the bus hit the motorcycle from behind (as is common in such accidents), res ipsa loquitur applies. The bus driver's negligence is self-evident, and no contributory negligence can be attributed to the pillion rider.
supporting.why_it_matters: This provides a powerful argument if the facts support it. A rear-end collision by a bus against a motorcycle makes the bus driver's negligence self-evident, and the pillion rider's helmet status becomes irrelevant to causation.
supporting.quote: The finding, which is based on correct and proper appraisal of the evidence makes the maxim of res ipsa loquitur applicable to the facts of the present case because the things are so apparent that the question of contributory negligence does not arise.

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: Even in case of death of a minor school-going child, a total compensation of Rs. 3,75,000 is awarded (Rs. 2,25,000 loss of dependency + Rs. 75,000 non-pecuniary + Rs. 75,000 future prospects). The insurer's statutory liability to pay third-party compensation exists even if there is a policy breach.
supporting.fact_alignment: This case directly supports the principle that a minor child's death commands substantial compensation. The deceased in Satto was a young son of a widowed mother — analogous to our client's situation as parents of a deceased minor.
supporting.why_it_matters: Provides a floor for compensation even under the older framework. Under the more recent RK Malik/Sangeeta Devi framework (doc_022), the compensation would be even higher. Also confirms that the bus insurer's statutory liability to third parties is unaffected by any policy breach.
supporting.quote: This Court in catena of judgments... has held that even in case of death of a minor school going child a total compensation of Rs. 3,75,000/- is to be awarded (Rs. 2,25,000/- towards loss of dependency, Rs. 75,000/- towards non-pecuniary damages and Rs. 75,000/- towards future prospects).

adverse.title: Kamal S/O Shiv Ram vs Mursleem S/O Mohd. Akil
adverse.principle: Contributory negligence is established when the injured rider is proven to have been driving without a valid driving license and without wearing a helmet, warranting a 50% deduction from compensation.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will cite this to argue that the pillion rider's failure to wear a helmet constitutes contributory negligence, and will seek a 50% deduction from the compensation. The case applied a 50% deduction where all three occupants (driver and two pillion riders) were not wearing helmets.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: Critically, in Kamal the 50% deduction was applied primarily because the DRIVER had no licence AND no helmet — the driver's own negligence in riding without a licence was the main cause. The pillion riders' lack of helmets was a secondary factor. In our case, the deceased was a pillion rider (not the driver) and had no control over the motorcycle. A pillion rider's failure to wear a helmet does not cause or contribute to the accident itself — it may only affect the nature/severity of injuries. The insurer must prove that the lack of a helmet caused or contributed to the accident, not just to the injuries. Moreover, the 50% figure is not a fixed rule; it depends on the facts. A much lower deduction (if any) would be appropriate for a pillion rider. Also, this is a Tribunal-level decision with persuasive value only.
adverse.quote: The contributory negligence of injured is proved in view of testimony of PW-1 Kamal who categorically deposed... that he is the one who was driving the motorcycle... he did not have DL at the time of accident and they all three were not wearing the helmets. Keeping in view of circumstances of the case, the 50% of the total compensation amount is deducted towards contributory negligence.

adverse.title: National Insurance Co.Ltd. vs Harpreet Singh And Ors.
adverse.principle: Legal representatives of a deceased who was not earning and had no dependents may still claim compensation, but the quantum is limited to loss to estate, not loss of dependency.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will argue that since the deceased was a 16-year-old minor with no income and no dependents, the compensation should be minimal — limited to loss to estate with no dependency component. This could depress the award if the tribunal applies the adult framework rather than the child-specific RK Malik framework.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case does not concern a minor child. The RK Malik framework (as applied in Sangeeta Devi, doc_022) specifically addresses children with no proven earnings by using inflation-corrected notional income (Rs. 15,000 p.a. from the Second Schedule) and applying age-specific multipliers (18 for age 15-18), plus an equal amount as composite non-pecuniary damages. This yields a substantial award. The Harpreet Singh principle applies to adults with no dependents, not to minor children where the RK Malik framework is the governing authority.

priority_arguments: Lead with Sangeeta Devi (doc_022) for the compensation framework: the deceased was 16 (>15 but <18), so multiplier is 18, notional income is Rs. 15,000 p.a. inflation-corrected via CII, 1/3rd deduction, plus equal composite non-pecuniary damages. This yields a significantly higher award than the standard adult framework.

On contributory negligence: the burden of proof is on the insurer (doc_018). The deceased was a pillion rider, not the driver — he had no control over the motorcycle. The insurer must prove that the absence of a helmet caused or contributed to the accident, not just to the severity of injuries. This is a very high bar.
If the bus hit the motorcycle from behind, argue res ipsa loquitur (doc_023) — the bus driver's negligence is self-evident and contributory negligence does not arise.
If there is an eye-witness, rely on doc_006 (Meena) to argue that consistent oral testimony cannot be overridden by assumptions from a police sketch or site plan.

The Kamal case (doc_009) is distinguishable: the 50% deduction there was primarily for the driver riding without a licence, and the pillion riders' lack of helmets was a secondary factor. A pillion rider's helmet status does not cause the accident.
Alternatively, rely on Satto (doc_033) which held that even for a minor school-going child, minimum compensation is Rs. 3.75 lakhs, providing a floor.
strategy.compensation_range: Approximately Rs. 6-12 lakhs (depending on the year of accident and applicable CII), computed as: inflation-corrected notional income (Rs. 15,000 × CII_year/331), rounded, minus 1/3rd personal expenses, × multiplier 18, plus an equal amount as composite non-pecuniary damages. Plus funeral expenses and interest at 7.5-9% p.a. from the date of petition. For a recent accident (CII ~ 363 for 2023-24): notional income ~Rs. 16,450 p.a., loss to estate = (16,450 × 2/3 × 18) = ~Rs. 1,97,400, doubled = ~Rs. 3,94,800, plus funeral expenses ~Rs. 16,500 = ~Rs. 4.1 lakhs. However, if the tribunal applies the more generous RK Malik formula with higher inflation adjustment, the figure could be higher.
strategy.compensation_reasoning: Under the RK Malik framework as applied in Sangeeta Devi (doc_022), for a child aged >15 but <18, the multiplier is 18. The notional income of Rs. 15,000 p.a. (Second Schedule) is inflation-corrected using the CII for the financial year of the accident. After deducting 1/3rd for personal expenses, the balance is capitalised using multiplier 18. An equal amount is added as composite non-pecuniary damages (covering conventional heads and future prospects). The Satto case (doc_033) provides a floor of Rs. 3.75 lakhs for a minor child's death even under the older framework.
risks: The insurer will cite Kamal (doc_009) to argue for a 50% contributory negligence deduction for not wearing a helmet. Counter: the deceased was a pillion rider, not the driver; the helmet's absence did not cause the accident.

The insurer will argue that a minor with no income should get minimal compensation under Harpreet Singh (doc_007). Counter: Sangeeta Devi (doc_022) provides a specific framework for children that yields substantial compensation.

If the motorcycle rider (who survived) is found to have been negligent (e.g., riding without a licence, speeding), the insurer may argue that the pillion rider should have known better. Counter: a 16-year-old pillion rider cannot be expected to assess the driver's competence; the duty to ensure a valid licence is on the rider/driver, not the pillion.
The insurer may challenge the multiplier or the notional income figure. Counter: the multiplier of 18 for age 15-18 is well-established in RK Malik and Sangeeta Devi.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: File a claim petition under Section 166 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 before the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal having jurisdiction over the place of accident. Claim compensation as per the RK Malik / Sangeeta Devi framework. Also claim interim compensation under Section 140 (no-fault liability) of Rs. 50,000, which is payable regardless of negligence.

caveats: doc_001 (Neelam Devi) — about pay-and-recover for hazardous goods endorsement. Entirely unrelated to minor child compensation or helmet contributory negligence.
doc_003 (Parvathi Hebbar) — about driving licence renewal lapse and pay-and-recover. Not relevant; our claim is against the bus insurer, not about the motorcycle driver's licence.
doc_016 (Reserved On vs State of HP) — criminal revision about a passenger falling from a bus while boarding. Criminal negligence standard, not civil compensation or contributory negligence.
doc_017 (Sanjay vs State of Haryana) — criminal conviction for rash driving. Not relevant to civil compensation.
doc_027 (Chennamma) — about driving licence endorsement for heavy goods vehicle. Not relevant.
doc_028 (Sukumarbai) — about gratuitous passengers in a private vehicle for hire. Not relevant; our deceased was a pillion rider on a motorcycle hit by a bus — a third party vis-à-vis the bus.
doc_029 (Minor Mahesh Kanubhai) — about gratuitous passengers in goods vehicle/tractor. Not relevant for the same reason.
doc_031 (Laxmi Narain Dhut) — about own-damage claims vs third-party claims. Not relevant.
doc_038 (Crown Consultants) — consumer dispute about claim filing delay. Not relevant.
doc_051 (Yashpal Chaudhrani) — criminal quashing for economic offences. Not relevant.
doc_054 (Chinnasamy) — civil suit for specific performance. Not relevant.

The corpus does not contain any Supreme Court judgment directly holding that a pillion rider's failure to wear a helmet constitutes contributory negligence. The only case on point (Kamal, doc_009) is a Tribunal-level decision where the 50% deduction was driven primarily by the driver's lack of a licence, not solely by the helmet issue.

The corpus does not contain any judgment quantifying the exact compensation for a 16-year-old deceased minor using the RK Malik framework. Sangeeta Devi (doc_022) applied it to a 10-year-old; the principles are directly transferable but the specific figures will depend on the CII for the year of the accident.

No judgment in the corpus addresses the specific question of whether a pillion rider's failure to wear a helmet can be contributory negligence when the accident was caused solely by the bus driver's negligence. The causation chain is critical: lack of a helmet does not cause the accident, it may only affect injury severity.

On a perusal of the definition of word 'tractor' shows that the tractor itself is not able to carry any

In view of the above, we observed that the trailer/trolley, which is attached with the tractor is a part

The brief facts of the case in narrow compass are that on 02.12.2000, one Sri Arvind Kumar was
going on scooter to see off his relative. When he reached near Hyderabad Paisara, one Tractor No.
U.P. 35-B 1649 took a sharp turn. The Iron Rods loaded in the trolley (trailer) attached to the tractor
in question hits the deceased Arvind Kumar, who died on the spot. The FIR was lodged. The Tractor
was insured but trolley was not insured. So, the liability was fixed against the owner of the Tractor
i.e. appellant by the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal for Rs.1,18,850/-. Being aggrieved, he filed the
present appeal.
During the course of argument, learned counsel for the appellant submits that the trailer is the part
of the tractor and tractor was duly insured. Independently, the tractor or trolley is not of any use.
With the tractor, some equipments or trolley will have to be attached for the purpose of agricultural
activity. He further submits that trailer/trolley falls within the definition of the vehicles, as such, it is
an attachment made to the prime mover of tractor and it has no independent driving system.
Therefore, it is not required to be insured under the provisions of Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 and
insurance company is liable to pay the compensation.
According to the appellant's counsel, deceased was driving the scooter without holding any valid
license.

n the instant case, the tractor in question (No. U.P. 35-B 1649) was duly insured with the insurance
company. Admittedly, no separate premium was paid for the trolley. This was the specific defense
taken by the insurance company.
The Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of National Insurance Company v. Chinnamma and others;
2004 (3) TAC 577 SC defines the meaning of tractor and trailer, which reads as under:
"Tractor: 'tractor' means a motor vehicle which is not itself constructed to carry any
load (other than equipment used for the purpose of population); but excludes a road
roller.
Trailer: trailer means by any vehicle, other than a semi-trailer and a side-car, drawn
or intended to be drawn by a motor vehicles."
In the case of Parsottambhai Kanbhai v. Panchiben alias Ratanben, 1977 A.C.J. 441 Hon'ble Gujarat
High Court made an observation that "As the trailer is included in the expression motor vehicle, it
was required to be insured.
The word 'trailer' was separately defined from the inclusive definition, which was made. In such an
event, the meaning assigned to the respective words has to be culled out. As can be seen from the
various definitions like articulated vehicles, contract carriage, goods carriage, heavy goods vehicle,
heavy passenger, motor vehicle, invalid carriage, maxi cab, motor cab, motor car, motor cycle,
omnibus, private service vehicles, they were defined as motor vehicles including tractor, but the
trailer was defined as motor vehicle, which was intended to drawn by a motor vehicle. Thus, it is

doc_002 (Liyakat Ali) — about tractor used for non-agricultural purposes (transporting bricks). Entirely unrelated to our case (bus vs motorcycle, pillion rider death).

doc_017 (Sanjay vs State of Haryana) — criminal conviction for rash driving. Not relevant to civil compensation.
doc_027 (Chennamma) — about driving licence endorsement for heavy goods vehicle. Not relevant.
doc_028 (Sukumarbai) — about gratuitous passengers in a private vehicle for hire. Not relevant.
doc_029 (Minor Mahesh Kanubhai) — about gratuitous passengers in goods vehicle/tractor. Not relevant.
doc_031 (Laxmi Narain Dhut) — about own-damage claims vs third-party claims. Not relevant.
doc_038 (Crown Consultants) — consumer dispute about claim filing delay. Not relevant.

doc_054 (Chinnasamy) — civil suit for specific performance. Not relevant.

The corpus does not contain any Supreme Court judgment directly holding that a pillion rider's failure to wear a helmet constitutes contributory negligence. The only case on point (Kamal, doc_009) is a Tribunal-level decision where the 50% deduction was driven primarily by the driver's lack of a licence, not solely by the helmet issue.
